items.title: Connecting the Dots: Securing the Overlooked Corners of the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) Supply Chain
items.one_liner: The ChainDrop npm worm highlights how attackers poison CI/CD pipelines and developer environments to harvest cloud secrets and propagate malware.
items.summary: Recent threat intelligence from Unit 42 highlights a massive shift in supply-chain attacks toward poisoning the software development lifecycle (SDLC) rather than targeting finished applications. A notable example is the ChainDrop npm worm, which infected over 400 packages—including keyv and cacheable-request—using a stealthy three-step chain involving modified preinstall hooks and the Bun runtime. The worm reads live process memory from GitHub Actions runners to harvest temporary OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens and credentials, backdoors developer tools like VS Code, and uses Ethereum blockchain transactions for dynamic command-and-control communication. Because modern applications are assembled from thousands of indirect open-source dependencies, these attacks compromise developer laptops, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud environments before code ever reaches production.
items.bottom_line: The ChainDrop worm infected over 400 npm packages by exploiting preinstall scripts to harvest GitHub Actions tokens and backdoor developer environments.

items.title: Named Pipes Under Attack: Securing Windows Interprocess Communication
items.one_liner: Treat Windows named pipes as exposed network interfaces to prevent local privilege escalation attacks across different security contexts.
items.summary: Windows named pipes, frequently used for interprocess communication between privileged services and user-facing desktop applications, are frequently mismanaged under the unsafe assumption that local communication is implicitly trusted. Because local environments host unrelated processes operating under various security contexts, an exposed named pipe can act as an unauthorized API to privileged functionality if permissions are overly permissive. Developers must implement strict access controls, avoid broad 'Everyone' or 'Authenticated Users' permissions, and ensure authentication, authorization, and impersonation routines are handled securely to prevent privilege escalation.
items.bottom_line: Assuming Windows named pipes are secure because they are local creates severe privilege escalation risks, requiring strict explicit access controls and input verification.

items.title: How an Emerging Industrial Protocol Family Could Put OT at Risk
items.one_liner: Unsecured Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) protocols in industrial automation expose operational technology to physical process manipulation.
items.summary: Recent research presented at Black Hat USA by Nozomi Networks researchers reveals that unencrypted Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) protocols used in industrial automation can be exploited to manipulate physical operational technology (OT) processes. TSN protocols orchestrate deterministic traffic flow over standard Ethernet to prevent communication collisions in safety-critical manufacturing environments. However, researchers demonstrated that lack of robust security controls allows attackers to tamper with process variables—such as starting or stopping robotic arms—or inject subtle timing drifts into synchronization clocks that cause damaging, delayed failures.
key_facts: Acquisition value: ~$1 billion (Mitsubishi Electric and Nozomi Networks)
items.bottom_line: Vulnerabilities in Time-Sensitive Networking protocols allow attackers to remotely manipulate industrial machinery and inject dangerous clock drifts into OT networks.

items.summary: Researchers captured photographs of a shoal of about 100 neon flying squid rising unexpectedly from the Pacific Ocean around 370 miles from Tokyo and gliding near a boat for about 30 metres.
